analysis.one_liner: Cuts the federal corporate income tax rate from 35% to 18%.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the corporate tax rate to 18% never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the corporate income tax from a graduated rate that topped out at 35% to a flat 18% tax on corporate profits, including for personal service corporations. It would have taken effect for tax years starting after 2010. It was introduced with no cosponsors, sent to the tax-writing committee, and nothing ever happened to it.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations, and their owners and executives, would keep more of every dollar of profit: a company would pay 18 cents of tax per dollar of profit instead of up to 35 cents. The biggest winners would be the most profitable corporations, which pay the top rate today.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the graduated corporate rate with a flat 18% rate on corporate taxable income, down from 35% at the top.
Also cuts the top rate for personal service corporations (law firms, accounting firms, and similar companies) from 35% to 18%.
Applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2010, and makes matching changes to related provisions that reference the 35% rate.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect substantially less from corporate taxes, meaning the difference has to be made up by other taxpayers, by cutting spending, or by adding to the debt. Households and smaller businesses that pay personal income taxes would bear more of the load.
analysis.who_pays_short: Other taxpayers and the federal treasury

drawbacks.text: Cutting the top corporate rate from 35% to 18% would roughly cut corporate tax receipts, leaving a large hole in federal revenue that someone must fill through other taxes, less spending, or more borrowing.
The bill cuts rates with no offset at all — it contains only the rate reduction, no provision to replace the lost revenue, so its full cost would fall on the deficit or on other taxpayers.
The largest, most profitable corporations get the most benefit, since they are the ones actually paying the top 35% rate; companies with little or no profit get little.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but flows to corporations and their shareholders, who are disproportionately higher-income. The cost — a much smaller corporate tax base — is spread across everyone who pays federal taxes or relies on federal programs. Weighed honestly, this is a large, unoffset tax cut for a concentrated group, not a policy whose gains and costs balance out for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House tax committee the day it was introduced and never came back out — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Sessions introduced the bill on March 3, 2011.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No cosponsors signed on, and the committee took no further action — no markup or vote was ever scheduled — so the bill died at the end of the 112th Congress in January 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations are not better off, because the rate cut never happened. The federal treasury simply kept the 35% corporate rate, and no taxpayer paid for a new revenue hole. For a bill like this, its failure is essentially the status quo continuing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury and other taxpayers

for.name: Rep. Pete Sessions
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the corporate rate to 18% and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: The House committee that handles tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and took no further action; it never scheduled a markup or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: This was a Republican-sponsored bill with zero cosponsors from either party and no recorded support beyond the sponsor, so the record shows no coalition behind it.

industries.note: A drop from 35% to 18% is a near-half tax cut on every dollar of corporate profit, worth the most to the largest companies. The revenue given up would eventually have to be recovered from other taxpayers or borrowing, so the corporate gain comes directly at the public's cost.
